title: Celsus should have defended the doctrine he approves
source_text: Μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα ἀποδέχεται τοὺς τὴν ψυχὴν (??) τὸν νοῦν ἢ τὸ καλούμενον παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς πνευματικὸν ἢ λογικὸν πνεῦμα νοερὸν ἄγιον καὶ μακάριον ἢ ψυχὴν ζῶσαν ἐλπίζοντας ἕξειν αἰώνιον, καὶ σὺν θεῷ αὐτὸ ἔσεσθαι, προσίεται δὲ ὀρθῶς νομιζόμενον καὶ τὸ μὲν περὶ τῶν εὖ βιωσάντων ὡς εὐδαιμονησόντων δόγμα περὶ δὲ τῶν ἀδίκων ὡς πάμπαν αἰωνίοις κακοῖς συσχεθησομένων. καὶ τεθαύμακά γε τοῦ Κέλσου παρὰ πάντα τὰ λεγόμενα παρ᾿ αὐτῷ τὸ οὕτως ἐπιφερόμενον τοῖς προειρημένοις, ἐν ᾧ φησι· καὶ τούτου δὲ τοῦ δόγματος μήθ᾿ οὗτοι μήτ᾿ ἄλλος ἀνθρώπων μηδείς ποτε ἀποστῇ. καὶ ἐχρῆν γε αὐτὸν ὁρᾶν κατὰ Χριστιανῶν γράφοντα, οἷς ἡ πᾶσα ὑπόθεσίς ἐστι τῆς πίστεως ὁ θεὸς καὶ αἱ διὰ τοῦ Χριστοῦ περὶ τῶν δικαίων ἐπαγγελίαι καὶ περὶ τῶν ἀδίκων αἱ περὶ κολάσεως διδασκαλίαι, ὅτι τὸν ἀνατραπέντα Χριστιανὸν ἐκ τοῦ παραδέξασθαι τοὺς κατὰ Χριστιανῶν τοῦ Κέλσου λόγους εἰκός ἐστιν ἀποβαλόντα τὸν λόγον συναποβαλεῖν καὶ τὸ δόγμα, (οὗ) , φησὶ. μήτε Χριστιανοὶ ἀποσταῖεν μήτε μηδεὶς ἄλλος ἀνθρώπων. ἀλλὰ φιλανθρωπότερον οἶμαι Κέλσου Χρύσιππον πεποιηκέναι ἐν τῷ περὶ παθῶν θεραπευτικῷ, βουλόμενον θεραπεῦσαι τὰ πάθη ὡς κατεπείγοντα καὶ ἐνοχλοῦντα τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην ψυχὴν προηγουμένως μὲν τοῖς δοκοῦσιν αὐτῷ ὑγιέσι λόγοις δευτέρως δὲ καὶ τρίτως κἂν τοῖς μὴ ἀρέσκουσι τῶν δογμάτων· „κἂν γὰρ τρία,“ φησὶν, „ᾖ γένη τῶν ἀγαθῶν, καὶ οὕτω θεραπευτέον τὰ πάθη, οὐ περιεργαζόμενον ἐν τῷ καιρῷ τῆς φλεγμονῆς τῶν παθῶν τὸ προκαταλαβὸν δόγμα τὸν ὑπὸ τοῦ πάθους ἐνοχλούμενον, μή πως τῇ ἀκαίρῳ περὶ τὴν ἀνατροπὴν τῶν προκαταλαβόντων τὴν ψυχὴν δογμάτων σχολῇ ἡ ἐγχωροῦσα θεραπεία παραπόληται.“ φησὶ δὲ ὅτι, „κἂν ἡδονὴ ᾖ τὸ ἀγαθὸν, καὶ τοῦτο φρονῇ ὁ ὑπὸ τοῦ πάθους κρατούμενος, οὐδὲν ἧττον αὐτῷ βοηθητέον καὶ παραδεικτέον ὅτι καὶ τοῖς ἡδονὴν τἀγαθὸν καὶ τέλος τιθεμένοις ἀνομολογούμενόν ἐστι πᾶν πάθος.“ ἐχρῆν τοίνυν καὶ τὸν Κέλσον, ἅπαξ παραδέξασθαι λέγοντα τὰ περὶ τῶν εὖ βιωσάντων δόγματα ὡς εὐδαιμονησόντων καὶ περὶ τῶν ἀδίκων ὡς πάμπαν αἰωνίοις κακοῖς συσχεθησομένων, ἀκολούθως ἑαυτῷ ποιεῖν καὶ, εἰ οἷόν τ᾿ ἦν, μετὰ τὸν φαινόμενον αὐτῷ προηγούμενον λόγον ἐπικατασκευάσαι καὶ διὰ πλειόνων ἀποδεῖξαι ὅτι ἀληθῶς οἱ ἄδικοι πάμπαν αἰωνίοις κακοῖς συσχεθήσονται καὶ οἱ εὖ βιώσαντες εὐδαιμονήσουσι.
pass_a_gloss: After these he accepts (ἀποδέχεται) those hoping the soul [or] the mind or what is called among them spiritual (πνευματικόν) or rational spirit (λογικὸν πνεῦμα), intellectual (νοερόν), holy and blessed, or living soul, to have eternal, and that it will be with God; and he admits (προσίεται) as rightly held the doctrine about those who lived well as going to be happy, and about the unjust as going to be held fast (συσχεθησομένων) altogether by eternal evils. And I have marvelled (τεθαύμακα) at Celsus beyond all he says at what is added to the foregoing, where he says: and from this doctrine let neither these nor any other of men ever depart. He ought to have seen, writing against Christians, for whom the whole foundation (ὑπόθεσις) of the faith (πίστις) is God and the promises (ἐπαγγελίαι) through Christ concerning the just and the teachings (διδασκαλίαι) about punishment (κόλασις) concerning the unjust, that the Christian overturned (ἀνατραπέντα) by accepting Celsus's arguments (λόγους) against Christians, likely, having thrown away (ἀποβαλόντα) the word/faith (λόγον), throws away together (συναποβαλεῖν) also the doctrine from which, he says, neither Christians nor any other of men should depart. But more humanely (φιλανθρωπότερον) I think than Celsus Chrysippus acted in the Therapeutic (θεραπευτικῷ) [book] on passions (παθῶν), wishing to heal (θεραπεῦσαι) the passions as pressing (κατεπείγοντα) and troubling (ἐνοχλοῦντα) the human soul, first (προηγουμένως) by arguments seeming sound (ὑγιέσι) to him, secondly and thirdly even by doctrines not pleasing (μὴ ἀρέσκουσι) him: For even if, he says, there are three kinds (γένη) of goods, so too the passions must be healed, not meddling (περιεργαζόμενον) at the time of inflammation (φλεγμονή) of passions with the doctrine that has preoccupied (προκαταλαβόν) the one troubled by passion, lest by untimely (ἀκαίρῳ) leisure/attention (σχολῇ) about the overturning (ἀνατροπή) of doctrines that preoccupied the soul the possible (ἐγχωροῦσα) cure (θεραπεία) be lost (παραπόληται). He says that, even if pleasure (ἡδονή) is the good, and the one mastered (κρατούμενος) by passion thinks this, no less he must be helped and shown that also to those setting pleasure as the good and end (τέλος) every passion is inconsistent (ἀνομολογούμενον). So Celsus too, having once said he accepts the doctrines about those who lived well as going to be happy and about the unjust as held by eternal evils, ought to act consistently (ἀκολούθως) with himself and, if possible, after the argument appearing to him principal (προηγούμενον), to build further (ἐπικατασκευάσαι) and demonstrate (ἀποδεῖξαι) through more that truly the unjust will be held fast altogether by eternal evils and those who lived well will be happy.
pass_b_english: After this he approves of those who hope that the soul, or the mind, or what they call the spiritual or rational spirit, intellectual, holy and blessed, or the living soul (Genesis 2:7), will be theirs for ever and will be with God; and he admits as rightly held both the doctrine that those who have lived well will be happy and the doctrine that the unjust will be held wholly in the grip of eternal evils. And of all that Celsus says, what amazes me most is what he adds to these words, where he says: “And from this doctrine let neither these nor any other man ever depart.”

Writing against Christians, for whom the whole foundation of faith is God, and the promises made through Christ concerning the righteous, and the teachings about punishment concerning the unjust, he ought to have seen this: a Christian overthrown by accepting Celsus’s arguments against Christians would in all likelihood, in throwing away the teaching, throw away with it the very doctrine from which, he says, neither Christians nor any other man should depart.

But Chrysippus, I think, acted more humanely than Celsus in his Therapeutic book On the Passions. Wishing to heal the passions, since they press hard upon the human soul and trouble it, he does so first by the arguments that seemed sound to him, but secondly and thirdly even by doctrines that did not please him. “For even if there are three kinds of goods,” he says, “even so the passions must be healed; one should not, while the passions are inflamed, busy oneself with the doctrine that has already taken hold of the one troubled by passion, so that the cure that is still possible may not be lost through untimely labour over overturning the doctrines that have already seized the soul.” And he says: “Even if pleasure is the good, and the one mastered by passion thinks so, he must none the less be helped and shown that every passion is inconsistent even with the views of those who make pleasure the good and the end.”

Celsus too, then, once he had said that he accepted the doctrines that those who have lived well will be happy and that the unjust will be held wholly in the grip of eternal evils, ought to have acted consistently with himself, and, if he could, after what seemed to him the principal argument, to have built further upon it and to have shown with further arguments that the unjust will truly be held wholly in the grip of eternal evils and that those who have lived well will be happy.

choices.choice: The staged text marks a gap (??) between τὴν ψυχήν and τὸν νοῦν; an ἤ (‘or’) is clearly wanted from the parallel in 8.49, and the English supplies it. ἐλπίζοντας ἕξειν αἰώνιον, καὶ σὺν θεῷ αὐτὸ ἔσεσθαι: the hopers expect to have the soul or mind eternal and that it will be with God; rendered ‘will be theirs for ever and will be with God’, as in 8.49. ‘Living soul’ repeats Celsus’s use of the Genesis 2:7 phrase, cited inline as in 8.49. In ‘throwing away the teaching’ the Greek is τὸν λόγον, Origen’s term for the Christian teaching as a whole (not πίστις, so not rendered ‘faith’). (οὗ) before φησί is an editorial supplement, followed. Chrysippus, Therapeutic book of On the Passions (the fourth book of his Περὶ παθῶν); the passage is collected as Stoicorum Veterum Fragmenta 3.474, and Origen cites it also at 1.64; the fragment reference is given here only, not inline. ‘Three kinds of goods’ is the Peripatetic division (goods of soul, body and external fortune), which a Stoic did not accept. ‘First... secondly and thirdly’ (προηγουμένως... δευτέρως δὲ καὶ τρίτως) kept as in the Greek. διὰ πλειόνων ἀποδεῖξαι rendered ‘shown with further arguments’.
'will have eternal life and will be with God' -> 'will be theirs for ever and will be with God' (ἐλπίζοντας ἕξειν αἰώνιον: 'life' was added; matches 8.49)
'held fast altogether by eternal evils' -> 'held wholly in the grip of eternal evils' (three places)
'in throwing away the faith' -> 'in throwing away the teaching' (Greek τὸν λόγον, not τὴν πίστιν)
'which press hard upon' -> 'since they press hard upon' (ὡς κατεπείγοντα gives Chrysippus's reason)

Chrysippus quotation: 'at the time when the passions are inflamed' -> 'while the passions are inflamed'; 'lest by untimely attention ... be lost' -> 'so that the cure that is still possible may not be lost through untimely labour over...' (archaic 'lest' and Greek order removed, sense kept)
'shown at greater length' -> 'shown with further arguments' (διὰ πλειόνων)
